newsitem.title: GERMANY: MGAM crisis forces Deutsche review.
newsitem.headline: MGAM crisis forces Deutsche review.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank AG determined to prove itself as a global investment bank, faces the task of sharpening internal controls to prevent a repeat of a crisis at its London fund management arm.

Analysts said on Thursday that Deutsche must act to counter the blow dealt to the aggressively expansionist bank's image by possible irregularities in three funds run by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) in London.

"Something like this can never be allowed to happen again. If Deutsche really wants to be a global player in investment banking, then its control mechanisms must keep in step with its growth," said Vereinsbank analyst Natalia Grasegger.

The crisis erupted on Monday with the suspension of three funds operated by MGAM, part of Deutsche's investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, pending a probe by British securities watchdog IMRO and MGAM itself.

The funds returned to trading on Thursday but only after Deutsche was forced to buy 180 million pounds ($282.4 million) in securities from the funds -- with no certainty of getting its money back from the portfolio.
Deutsche has also issued a legal injunction against fund manager Peter Young and suspended his colleague Stewart Armer.

It was unclear on Thursday whether more heads would roll, but Deutsche confirmed it would review the possible supervision lapses that allowed Young to maintain a portfolio thought to contain a high level of unlisted Scandinavian securities.

"Of course we will be discussing the situation (with risk control) and we will be seeing how we can improve matters. This is a task for both for us, the Deutsche Bank group, and for Morgan Grenfell," said a Deutsche spokesman.
MGAM, with 70 billion pounds under management, holds half of Deutsche's fund management portfolio.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell itself, which Deutsche bought six years ago and which reports to the German management board on London supervisory issues, was more circumspect. It said it was too early to say if controls needed to be tightened.
Analysts said Deutsche had so far handled the situation well, particularly praising its move to absorb the financial damage by buying up the questionable securities.
"The goodwill they have shown displays how seriously they want to be taken in this business," said Bank Julius Baer, Frankfurt, analyst Manfred Piontke.
"As an exercise in damage control, I think this will be successful," said Matthew Czepliewicz, analyst at Salomon Brothers, London.
However Konrad Becker, analyst at Merck, Finck, cautioned: "The fact that they (Deutsche) have taken up the slack does not mean this was not a bad thing to happen at all."
Becker and other analysts said Deutsche had invested too much in expanding its asset management business in London without paying enough attention to the business itself.
A further problem could have been the difficulty of merging disparate groups of high-flying personnel which Deutsche Morgan Grenfell has poached from rivals to support its expansion.

"One can never have 100 percent protection if someone actually wants to dupe a bank. But here it seems that Deutsche's efforts in the back office, especially things like risk control, did not keep pace with their business expansion and that is what has caused this problem," Becker said.

Deutsche itself downplayed the crisis, its spokesman saying: "It is important to see here that no investors have been hurt. All this meant for investors was a loss of liquidity in the funds for three days. No further harm has been done." ($1=.6373 Pound)
